newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's Khatami likely to lose cabinet nominees.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Khatami likely to lose cabinet nominees.

text.p: Iran's President Mohammad Khatami is expected to lose at least one of his cabinet nominees in a parliamentary vetting process which starts on Tuesday, Iranian newspapers and analysts said on Monday.

But despite the possible loss of critical ministers in key domestic portfolios, the 54-year-old moderate cleric will still emerge with the majority of his cabinet intact and his election mandate for change undamaged, analysts said.
"There is a consensus among deputies that the majority of the proposed ministers will get the vote of confidence," influential conservative deputy Mohammad Reza Bahonar told the daily Resalat.

The conservative-dominated 270-seat Majlis, or parliament, is expected to vote on Wednesday on Khatami's 22 cabinet nominees after debating in three five-hour sessions, parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri has said.
Nateq-Nouri on Monday told Iran's news agency IRNA: "Everything is possible. However, it is not possible to predict which of them will get the vote of confidence and who will not."
A newspaper said Khatami would circumvent rejection of some candidates by appointing them as vice presidents who would become de facto in charge of the ministries.

"If any of President Khatami's proposed ministers are rejected by the Majlis, the President will then appoint the rejected minister, or ministers, as vice president," the Iran News daily said on Monday.

Khatami has said that vice presidents are members of the cabinet in addition to the 22 portfolios and analysts said it was likely that he would also appoint vice presidents for youth affairs and women's issues.
At least some of the proposed ministers are expected to present their programme in person to the parliament.
Khatami has said he has a list of alternatives for cabinet posts.
Strong opposition is expected from conservative factions in parliament to Khatami's proposed minister of culture Ataollah Mohajerani and interior minister designate Abdollah Nouri.

His proposed agriculture minister Issa Kalantari has also come under fire from conservative newspapers while Khatami has already conceded to pressure on his appointments as intelligence and defence ministries, analysts said.

"Opponents try to weaken President Khatami's cabinet so that a while they can claim that the cabinet is not functioning," Faezeh Hashemi, parliament deputy and daughter of former president Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, told the Akhbar newspaper.

The culture ministry has emerged as a battleground between Khatami's supporters who want to breathe more freedoms into the 18-year-old republic, and conservatives who see the ministry as the main weapon against a "Western cultural invasion".
The ministry has power over the diversity of media, books, films and music allowed in the country.
Mohajerani in particular has become a lightning rod for conservatives and hardliners for his support in 1990 of a resumption of talks with the United States.
"If such a person takes over the ministry of guidance (culture), the cultural independence of the country will be damaged," deputy Jahanbakhsh Mohebbi told Resalat newspaper on Sunday.
The interior ministry has influence over the conduct of elections and the appointment of provincial governors.
Khatami's next task after completing his cabinet will be to begin preparations to draw up the next budget, which will also have to be approved by parliament.
Revenues are already falling behind government forecasts because of a downturn in world oil prices, and the economy remains racked by double-digit inflation and unemployment.

Khatami was swept into power during national elections in May after scooping the votes of Iranian youth, women and the middle class who saw him as a leader able to inject social and economic freedoms in to the stern Islamic state.
Khatami crushed Nateq-Nouri at the polls, getting nearly 20 million votes compared to the speaker's seven million.
Ultimate power, particularly in foreign relations, in this country of 60 million people rests firmly in the hands of supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
